01

Slow Race Car

Project
1.1.4, Mechanical Design unit
Challenge
Build the slowest vehicle in the class
Platform
VEX V5
Wiring
Smart Motor on Port 5, Bumper Switch on Port A

Overview

Slow Race Car was my first robotics project in Principles of Engineering. The challenge was to build the slowest possible VEX vehicle to race against my classmates. The vehicle uses a VEX V5 Brain, a battery pack, a Smart Motor on Port 5, and a Bumper Switch on Port A. The Bumper Switch turns the motor on and off.

The project focuses on how gearing changes speed. A gear train with a higher ratio slows the output and increases torque, so I used gears to slow the car down while keeping it moving across the course marked with tape. My gear train has three axles: one with an 84-tooth gear, one with a 12-tooth and an 84-tooth gear, and one with a 12-tooth gear. Each gear pair has a ratio of 7:1 (84 ÷ 12), so together they slow the motor about 49 times and increase torque.

Problem statement

Design and build a vehicle that travels a set distance more slowly than every other vehicle in the class. The car had to use simple gear trains and include all required components. The difficulty was making the car slow but still able to move: with poorly aligned gears or too much friction, it could stall before finishing the course.

Design process

  1. AskHow does gearing change the speed of a motor? Connecting a small gear to a larger one slows the output and increases torque, which is what a slow car needs.
  2. ImagineI looked at the VEX parts available, including axles, bearings, gears, wheels, and metal pieces, and thought about how to connect them to the motor.
  3. PlanI planned a gear train to slow the motor down and decided where to place the motor, Brain, battery, and bumper switch on the frame.
  4. CreateI built the car from VEX parts, then loaded the motor code onto the V5 Brain with VEXcode V5 and tested it on a course marked with tape.
  5. ImproveMy first gear train had gears that were placed incorrectly, so I rebuilt it. I also found that the motor would not fit underneath the frame. A student from another class suggested adding an extra axle and gear on top of the frame to link the motor to the gear train. This made the car work, but the extra gear did not mesh well with the others.

Testing

I tested the car on a course marked with tape. It ran very slowly, as planned, and worked for a while. Then the gears slowly drifted apart and the car stopped. The test showed me that a gear train can slow a car down, but the gears must stay properly meshed.

Reflection

What went well

My car was very slow, which was the goal, and it ran for a while before stopping. I fixed the gear problem from my first attempt and learned how to load code onto the V5 Brain.

What I would improve

Next time I would sketch my design before building and make sure every gear meshes properly and stays in place. I would also record the car's time and compare it with my classmates' results.

What I learned

Gearing trades speed for torque. Gears must mesh correctly or they drift apart. Checking that parts physically fit is part of planning, and asking for help can lead to a better solution.

Next projectTug-of-War
02

Tug-of-War

Project
1.1.5, Mechanical Design unit
Challenge
Pull with the greatest force possible
Platform
VEX V5 kit
Focus
Mass, friction, and gearing

Overview

Tug-of-War was my second robotics project in Principles of Engineering. The challenge was to design and build a VEX vehicle that could pull with the greatest force possible and compete in tug-of-war battles. I used a VEX V5 kit and masking tape to mark the course.

The project focuses on how mass, friction, and gearing affect pulling strength. A vehicle with more torque and better grip on the floor can pull harder.

Problem statement

Design and build a prototype that can win a tug-of-war by pulling as strongly as possible, using what I learned about mass, friction, and gearing. The difficulty was balancing these factors: a vehicle needs enough torque to pull, but also enough grip on the floor, or its wheels will slip.

Torque

Gears multiply the motor's turning force so the wheels can pull harder.

Mass

More weight pressing down on the drive wheels gives them more grip.

Friction

Grip between wheels and floor decides whether force becomes pulling or slipping.

Design process

  1. AskWhat makes a vehicle strong in a tug-of-war? Pulling strength depends on the torque from the gears, the weight of the vehicle, and the friction between the wheels and the floor.
  2. ImagineI looked at the VEX parts available and thought about how to arrange the motor, gears, and wheels to get more pulling force.
  3. PlanI decided to reuse my Slow Race Car gear train, which already increases torque, and add grip.
  4. CreateI reused my Slow Race Car build, which has one motor, and loaded the Tug-of-War code onto the V5 Brain.
  5. ImproveI made one change to my Slow Race Car build: I added rubber bands to the wheels to improve grip. My first attempt was incorrect because the rubber bands were also on an axle, so I fixed it. I did not change the gears or the mass.

Testing

I tested my vehicle against a classmate's vehicle. The two vehicles were connected by a steel bar and pulled in opposite directions across a taped centerline. I did not measure the pulling force with the Vernier sensor, so I do not have force readings in Newtons.

Reflection

What went well

I reused my gear train, which already increases torque, and after I fixed my first mistake, the rubber bands gave the wheels more grip. I also learned how to load and run code for a new challenge.

What I would improve

My vehicle pulled only barely. Its gears did not mesh well, which probably wasted force. Next time I would build a gear train made for pulling, add weight over the drive wheels for more grip, measure the pulling force with the sensor, repeat each test several times, and record the results so I can compare changes.

What I learned

Gearing can increase pulling force but lowers speed. Mass and friction affect how well a vehicle can pull. A build made for one challenge may not suit another, and testing and measuring are how a design gets better.

Learning by building

I'm Zhanylai Madakimova, a student taking Principles of Engineering. Before this class I had never built or programmed a robot, so every project here is something new for me.

I'm interested in how gears and simple machines turn motion into speed or force. In my first projects, I built prototypes directly from the VEX parts and learned by testing them and making changes. In future projects, I plan to sketch my ideas before building.

This portfolio brings together my first projects from Principles of Engineering. Each one shows how I approached the design challenge, how I tested my prototype, and what I learned from the results. It will keep growing throughout the year as I add new projects and improve my documentation.
